newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan central banker cool on private forex plan.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan central banker cool on private forex plan.

text.p: Taiwan central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong gave a cool response on Tuesday to a top economic policymaker's proposal to let local and foreign banks manage some of the island's huge foreign exchange reserves.
"This is only the opinion of the Council for Economic Planning and Development," Sheu told reporters. "It does not represent the central bank's position."
Sheu was referring to a proposal floated on Tuesday by Schive Chi, vice chairman of the Council for Economic Planning and Development, a powerful policymaking arm of the ruling cabinet.
Sheu did not say explicitly that the central bank would oppose Schive's proposal, but made clear that he as bank governor was not a strong supporter.

Sheu said the central bank already allows some foreign financial institutions to manage up to five percent of Taiwan's more than US$86 billion in reserves, the world's third largest, but that the experience had been less than successful.
"The return has not been as good as that under central bank management," Sheu said.
Sheu kept the central bank's options open.
"We can certainly study the plan and gradually liberalise," he said.

Schive, in a telephone interview, told Reuters that aside from the forex management scheme, the cabinet was considering allowing foreign and local banks to participate for the first time in management of Taiwan's huge central pension funds.

Schive said opening up management of the reserves and pension funds to the private sector are being considered as part of an aggressive liberalisation drive aiming to make Taiwan more attractive as an investment destination and as a site for international firms' Asia-Pacific operations centres.
Schive's council is the campaign's driving force.
Schive said the moves could help Taiwan catch up with Hong Kong and Singapore in the number of branches of foreign financial institutions.
The central bank now controls management of Taiwan's vast forex reserves, which rank third in the world behind Japan's and China's at $86.387 billion.
The state also controls the island's huge government employee pension fund and state labour insurance fund, participation in which is mandatory for Taiwan enterprises.
Taiwan's forex reserves fell in late 1995 and early 1996 as political tensions with rival China intensified into a military crisis in March, triggering heavy capital outflows.

Taiwan's foreign reserves peaked at $100.412 billion in June 1995 -- the same month that Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui angered Beijing with a private but high-profile U.S. visit, sparking tensions with both Taiwan and the United States.
As of October 15, Taiwan had allowed 42 foreign banks to set up 65 branches on the island, the Finance Ministry said.
